query: For an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy in its uniform, fine lamellar state, whose strength and plasticity remain below industrial application requirements, what single intervention could improve performance for fasteners exposed to extreme temperature fluctuations, long-term mechanical loading, room-temperature creep, and corrosive conditions? State the proposed intervention, mechanism, predicted outcome relative to the starting alloy, applicable operating and test boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with explicit falsification criteria.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored low‐temperature annealing treatment can induce the in situ precipitation of coherent L12 nanoparticles within the fcc lamellae, yielding improved strength and creep resistance without sacrificing ductility.
generation.material_initial_state: Uniform, fine lamellar AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA with coupled fcc/B2 phases as obtained by conventional casting.
generation.intervention: Subject the as‐cast alloy to a controlled low‐temperature annealing process (600–800°C) with precise time control to nucleate and grow coherent L12 precipitates within the fcc regions.
generation.conditions: Annealing conducted at 600–800°C for durations calibrated to achieve target nanoprecipitate sizes (<50 nm) and volume fractions (approximately 10–15%); testing under room temperature up to ~700°C under long-term mechanical loading, temperature cycling, and corrosive conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of coherent L12 nanoprecipitates embedded in the fcc lamellae, maintaining intact lamellar fcc/B2 interfaces and a refined microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The annealing process leverages slight supersaturation in the fcc phase to drive nucleation of fine L12 particles that hinder dislocation motion (via the Orowan mechanism) and improve resistance against creep and microcrack propagation.
generation.predicted_outcome: A marked increase in yield and tensile strength (targeting >10–15% improvement) with improved creep resistance, while ductility is maintained at industrially acceptable levels, enhancing performance in fasteners under extreme thermal and corrosive conditions.
generation.baseline: The as-cast alloy shows insufficient strength and creep resistance with a lamellar microstructure.
generation.boundary: Effective for applications operating from room temperature to ~700°C in cyclic and corrosive environments; the annealing parameters must be tightly controlled to avoid over-coarsening or lamellar degradation.
generation.uncertainty: The exact long-term stability of the precipitates under service conditions and their retention of coherency during cyclic loading remain to be established through detailed aging studies and in situ microstructural analyses.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples from the as-cast alloy and subject a set to the specified low‐temperature annealing treatment. Conduct mechanical tests (tensile, creep) and corrosion tests in chloride-containing solutions, comparing them with untreated controls.
measurements: Nanoprecipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction (TEM, in situ diffraction)
Yield and tensile strength, creep rate under constant load
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If annealed samples do not exhibit at least a 10–15% improvement in yield strength and reduced creep rate relative to untreated ones, or if precipitates coarsen detrimentally, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: As such, our alloy design strategy resulted in the discovery of an EHEA with a fine lamellar fcc/B2 structure and balanced high fracture strength and high ductility. This novel strategy is promising to solve the problems inhibiting the engineering application of HEAs as high-temperature materials, including the inferior castability and compositional segregation, and the conflict between high fracture strength and high ductility. In addition, this novel strategy also brought breakthrough to NiAl-based alloys in significantly enhancing the ductility at room temperature while simultaneously achieving the high strength. The EHEA concept, combining the advantages of both HEAs and eutectic alloys, and at the same time eliminating the disadvantages of these two types of alloys, leads to a promising new class of high-temperature alloys. Using this new alloy design strategy, an industrial scale HEA with uniform organizations and compositions can be prepared by the conventional casting method in a low cost way, allowing for large-scale industrial applications. In this work, we successfully achieve a superior strength–ductility combination in AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEAs by introducing two concurrent effects, the two-hierarchical constraint effect and the self-generated microcrack-arresting mechanisms. The underlying origin lying behind the observed mechanical response is the inherited lamellar geometry from the as-cast EHEA. It is known that grain refinement to the nano/ultrafine-grained regime can render material stronger, but this process is usually accompanied by a dramatic loss of ductility. However, with a composite lamellar architecture, the ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure in this study achieves an improved strength–ductility synergy. Phase decomposition is applied to optimize properties instead of just being a phase-instability phenomenon frequently observed in single-phase HEAs, which may encourage further research in this area. In addition, the AlCoCrFeNi2.1 EHEA could be simply processed to achieve properties that are an improvement over traditional TRIP (transformation-induced plasticity) and TWIP (twinning-induced plasticity) steels (Fig. 5). candidates.hypothesis: Microalloying with a trace element (e.g., Ti) combined with thermo-mechanical processing to promote fine L12 precipitate formation.

candidates.intervention: Apply a controlled surface nano-oxidation process—either via thermal oxidation in a controlled atmosphere or electrochemical oxidation—to develop a thin, adherent layer predominantly composed of Al2O3 and Cr2O3 on the alloy surface.
